title: What is M&A?
subtitle: Buying and merging companies
openingQuestion: What is the difference between a merger and an acquisition?
openingOptions: A merger combines two firms into one; an acquisition is one buying another
Acquisitions only happen with small companies
A merger is always bigger than an acquisition in terms of the size involved
explanation: Mergers and acquisitions differ on paper: one combines two businesses into a new legal entity, the other has the buyer taking control of the other side. In practice the line is blurry, and 'merger of equals' is often just a softer name for what is really an acquisition. What matters more than the label is who ends up holding decision-making power afterward, because that is what determines whether the integration actually works.

realWorldExample.description: Disney's $7.4 billion acquisition of Pixar is a classic example of M&A done well - Disney didn't just buy the animation technology, it kept Pixar's core creative team intact, generating genuine revenue synergy across a string of hit films afterward.

quiz.question: Why does most M&A fail to create value?
options: Overpaying and failing to execute post-merger integration
Because regulators usually block large deals partway through
Because the acquiring company is always forced to borrow to fund the deal
Because accounting rules require the entire purchase price to be expensed immediately
quiz.explanation: McKinsey research: 70% of M&A fails to meet expectations. The reasons: paying too much premium, illusory synergy, failed cultural integration, key talent leaving. The classic case: AOL-Time Warner in 2000 ($165B) - the largest failure in M&A history.

quiz.question: Why can an M&A deal be a "success" in terms of closing the transaction, yet still fail to create shareholder value years later?
options: Because the purchase price is only finally settled after three years of operation
Because value sits in integration, which happens after signing
Because shareholders only benefit once the business relists years after the original deal closed
Because auditors can require the deal's value to be written down later
quiz.explanation: Most academic research shows 50-70% of M&A deals fail to meet their stated value targets - and the most common cause isn't the price negotiation but post-merger integration: cultural conflict, losing key talent.

quiz.question: How does a merger differ from an acquisition?
options: Mergers apply to companies in the same industry, acquisitions to different industries
Mergers need cash, while acquisitions are paid in shares
A merger combines into a new legal entity, an acquisition buys control
Mergers are decided by shareholders, acquisitions by the board
quiz.explanation: A merger of equals combines two sides into one new legal entity; an acquisition is one side buying control of the other. In practice, most deals called "mergers" still have one side truly in charge.

quiz.question: What lesson does the $165 billion AOL-Time Warner deal in 2000 stand as?
options: Mergers between two different industries always fail later on
The bigger the deal, the higher the chance of success
Regulators should block every deal above $100 billion
A valuation built on expectations can evaporate very quickly
quiz.explanation: The deal closed right at the peak of the dot-com bubble, and most of the value paid was for a future that never arrived. Scale protected no one - it only made the mistake more expensive.

quiz.question: Key staff at the acquired company leave after the merger. Why is that dangerous?
options: Because the purchase value usually lies precisely in the capability they carried with them
Because the business has to pay very costly severance packages
Because M&A contracts require keeping staff unchanged for the first three years
Because hiring replacements raises selling and administrative expenses
quiz.explanation: Buying a software or consulting company is mostly buying its team. When they leave, what's left is just contracts and assets - and the premium already paid for the capability that just walked out the door.

keyTakeaways: Merger: combining as equals; Acquisition: buying and taking control
70% of M&A fails to create value for the acquirer
**Risk:** overpaying, culture clash, synergy that falls short of expectations

practicePrompt.question: Two similarly sized banks agree to merge into a new brand, with leadership split evenly between the two sides. A large tech company, meanwhile, buys a small startup outright and replaces the entire old leadership team. Which concepts do these two situations illustrate the difference between?
options: Merger: a union of equals (the two banks); Acquisition: one side buys and controls (the startup)
Both are examples of Acquisition because both involve combining two companies together
Both are examples of Merger because neither company was fully dissolved after the deal
Merger and Acquisition are just two names for the same type of deal, with no real difference
practicePrompt.explanation: Merger: combining as equals - two companies of equal standing joining into one new entity (like the two banks). Acquisition: buying and taking control - a larger company buys and takes control of a smaller one (like the tech company buying the startup, replacing the old leadership).

summary.keyIdea: Merger: combining as equals; Acquisition: buying and taking control
summary.commonMistake: Reading the concept as a phrase to memorize rather than a principle to apply to a real decision.
summary.action: 70% of M&A fails to create value for the acquirer

application.title: Apply it now
application.message: Look up a recent M&A deal you've heard of (e.g. in banking or retail), and work out whether it was really a merger or an acquisition in substance - regardless of what the press called it.
application.secondary: Telling the two apart correctly sharpens how you read business news.

sections.text: M&A (Mergers and Acquisitions) is the business of buying and merging companies - one of the fastest routes to growth in Corporate Finance, but also one of the riskiest, with most deals falling short of their original expectations.

A merger is when two companies A and B combine into a new company C, often described as a 'merger of equals'. An acquisition is when company A buys company B, and B becomes a subsidiary of A. In practice, the line between the two is quite blurry - many deals labeled a 'merger of equals' are, in substance, still an acquisition that neither side wants to call a takeover, for internal political reasons and brand image.
Why most M&A fails to create value

Research from McKinsey and other organizations shows that 50-70% of M&A deals fail to meet their stated value targets. A deal can 'succeed' in closing the transaction but still fail to create value years later, because closing is only the first step - real success depends on post-merger integration: retaining key talent, reconciling corporate cultures, and actually achieving the synergies promised when the deal was priced. The 2000 AOL-Time Warner deal, worth $165 billion, is the biggest failure in M&A history for exactly these reasons.

items: Why M&A fails: overpaying, cultural clash, synergy falling short of expectations
Rare success requires: a fair price, careful post-merger integration, retaining key talent
A classic success: Disney's acquisition of Pixar (2006, $7.4 billion) - kept the creative team intact, generated genuine revenue synergy across many hit films

lines: Closing an M&A deal is far easier than turning it into a genuinely profitable investment.
